name: Ririo
confidence_why: No source states where Ririo stress falls: Laycock 1982, the only first-hand description, says only that Ririo has essentially the same stress patterns as Babatana, and the one account of Babatana stress, Palmer 2014 (initial stress, left-aligned trochees, long vowels attract stress), describes Babatana rather than Ririo, so any Ririo rule is inferred, not observed.
catalog_citation: Laycock, Don. 1982. Metathesis in Austronesian: Ririo and other cases. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 269-281. Pacific Linguistics C-…
catalog_locator: Laycock 1982: p. 277 = PDF page 9 of (14 pp.), section 'Explanations for metathesis', second paragraph, last sentence; second sentence from p. 273 = PDF page 5…
catalog_quote: For Rotuman, the suggestion has been made by Churchward (1953), and again by Haudricourt (1958a,b) that the metathesis may have its basis in something like the stress-shifting rule in Tongan, where the stress shifts to the final vowel in definite forms of nouns (corresponding to the unmetathesised forms in Rotuman) (see also Thompson 1969) But no explanation of this type will work for Ririo, which has essentially the same stress patterns as Babatana. ... [p. 273] Whaley also claims contrastive vowel length for Babatana, but I am not entirely sure that this is not a function of stress and/or open versus closed syllables.
world_status: statement found in an open source

The quoted passage is there word for word: '.. For Rotuman, the suggestion has been made by Churchward (1953), and again by Haudricourt (1958a,b) that the metathesis may have its basis in something like the stress-shifting rule in Tongan, where the stress shifts to the final vowel in definite forms of nouns (corresponding to the unmetathesised forms in Rotuman) (see also Thompson 1969) But no explanation of this type will work for Ririo, which has essentially the same stress patterns as Babatana.' (The only differences are scanned spacing…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. Laycock only asserts that Ririo stress is essentially identical to that of the closely related Babatana (ruling out a Tongan/Rotuman-type stress-shift explanation for Ririo's CV metathesis). Babatana's stress pattern is not described in any accessible source either (Ray 1926 is silent per our earlier scan; Whaley 1962, cited by Laycock, is unpublished), so the statement does not resolve to a stress position.
new_statements.exceptions: None. p. 273 adds that Whaley's claimed contrastive vowel length in Babatana may be 'a function of stress and/or open versus closed syllables', implying stress interacts with length/syllable structure, but no rule is stated. Metathesised words carry an optional unwritten echo-vowel (p. 274), which would affect syllable count in citation forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark made in passing in a historical/metathesis paper based on Laycock's 1978 fieldwork at Susuka village (18 speakers); not a phonological description of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Laycock's data are from the Susuka village speakers (1978, 18 speakers) — the Ririo language proper (riri1237), no dialect distinction. Laycock stresses that imperfect speakers produce 'metathesised Babatana' rather than true Ririo (p. 278). The stress statement is relational to Babatana (baba1268), whose own stress is undescribed in accessible sources.

sources.note: Only Ririo-specific phonological description in print (orthography/phoneme table p. 273, metathesis rules pp. 274-276). On stress it says only (p. 277) that Ririo 'has essentially the same stress patterns as Babatana' (ruling out a Tongan/Rotuman-type stress-shift explanation of metathesis), and (p. 273) that Whaley's Babatana vowel length may be 'a function of stress and/or open versus closed syllables'. No statement of where stress falls.
Consonant and vowel inventories copied from Laycock 1982:273; no stress section.
